activities.anchor: a Punnett square at population scale
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the equilibrium proportions
activities.name: pgHWCloze

config.text: With two alleles A and a at frequencies p and q (p + q = %%0%%), random mating makes zygotes %%1%% AA : 2pq Aa : %%2%% aa — and the remarkable part is that these frequencies return %%3%% every generation, whatever the starting mix.
config.hint: Two alleles, frequencies sum to one; each homozygote gets the square of its allele's frequency.

activities.caption: pair each case with its selection geometry
activities.name: pgShapeMatch

config.prompt: Four case studies, four shapes of selection — pair them:

pairs.left: peppered moths' dark form rising with soot, falling as air cleaned
human birth weight — both extremes raise infant mortality
Darwin's finch bill-size bimodality on Santa Cruz island
the sickle-cell carrier fitter than either homozygote under malaria

config.why: Directional pushes an allele toward fixation; stabilising removes extremes and preserves the mean; disruptive favours both tails and can split a population; balancing holds a harmful allele at a computable equilibrium.

activities.anchor: Equilibrium settles where the two homozygote disadvantages balance
activities.caption: rank the genotypes — fitness under malaria
activities.name: pgFitnessOrder

config.prompt: Rank the three sickle-cell genotypes by fitness in a malarial region, fittest first:
items: AA homozygote — malaria-vulnerable (fitness ≈ 0.9 in endemic regions)
aa homozygote — severe sickle disease (fitness ≈ 0.25 historically)
config.why: The carrier is the fittest genotype, which is why selection cannot purge the allele: equilibrium sits near q ≈ 0.12, matching West African frequencies of 0.1–0.15. Remove malaria and the ranking collapses — selection drains the allele away.

config.prompt: Drift's signatures in the wild — file each fact:

items.label: the Amish's elevated Ellis–van Creveld syndrome from a few founders
Pingelap achromatopsia from a typhoon's ~20 survivors
northern elephant seals hunted to ~20–30 animals in the 1890s
cheetahs' immune genes so alike that skin grafts are accepted
an effective population of 50 losing ~18% heterozygosity in 20 generations
the probability an allele ultimately fixes equals its current frequency

config.why: Founders carry a skewed sample; bottlenecks crush diversity through a few breeders; and underneath both, the neutral theory's arithmetic — drift fixes alleles by pure chance (Kimura, 1968).

activities.anchor: the genetic damage from the 1890s bottleneck
activities.caption: same species, two ledgers — the census and the gene pool
activities.name: pgSealsCompare

config.prompt: Northern elephant seals, 100 years after the bottleneck — drag the divider between the two ledgers:

before.label: the census
before.text: 30,000-plus animals. The head count recovered within a century — by the numbers, the population looks fine.

after.label: the gene pool
after.text: Only ~20–30 breeders passed it on. Heterozygosity does not self-repair — the seals remain almost genetically uniform.

config.why: Drift's losses are restored only by mutation or gene flow, both painfully slow — which is why conservationists monitor Nₑ, not head counts.

activities.anchor: the fraction of total genetic variance held between populations
activities.caption: call the magnitude — F_ST for our species
activities.name: pgFstEstimate

config.prompt: F_ST is the fraction of total genetic variance held BETWEEN populations (near 0 = well-mixed, near 1 = isolated). For humans at the continental scale, roughly what is it?
config.why: ≈ 0.15: most human genetic variation is WITHIN any population — a result with direct bearing on how race and genetics intersect.
config.context: One migrant per generation between populations is enough, in theory, to prevent divergence by drift alone.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the studbook answer
activities.name: pgConserveSpot

config.prompt: This conservation-genetics answer contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: The inbreeding coefficient F climbs by 1/(2Nₑ) per generation in a closed population.
Inbreeding exposes recessive lethals and erodes fitness — litter sizes shrink, juvenile mortality climbs.
Studbooks therefore pair the most closely related lineages, to keep bloodlines pure.
Genetic rescue can reverse the spiral of inbreeding depression.
The Florida panther, down to ~25 cats, recovered after eight Texas females were introduced in 1995.
The targets: Nₑ near 50+ short-term, near 500+ to hold adaptive variation.
config.correction: Studbooks pair DISTANT lineages — the goal is heterozygosity, not purity of bloodline.
config.why: Pure bloodlines are exactly the problem: F measures excess homozygosity from mating among relatives, so the cure is mixing, as the panther's hybrid descendants showed with restored fitness.

activities.anchor: Human deep history shows the whole toolkit in one dataset
activities.caption: true or false — genes, geography and culture
activities.name: pgHistoryJudge

statements.s: Tibetan altitude adaptation rests on an EPAS1 haplotype traced to Denisovan introgression.
statements.why: Adaptation sourced from another archaic human species — gene flow caught across a species line.

statements.s: East African pastoralists carry the same −13910*T lactase variant as northern Europeans.
statements.why: They carry different variants with the same effect — convergent evolution, visible as parallel sweeps.

statements.s: Skin-pigmentation gradients are built from variants at half a dozen loci across continents.
statements.why: Polygenic adaptation, the opposite of a single-letter story.

statements.s: The lactase-persistence sweep took hundreds of thousands of years to reach near-fixation.
statements.why: A cultural innovation (dairying) rewrote the gene pool within historical time — ~7,500 years in northern European dairying populations.
